name: Nonverbal dominance

lead: Nonverbal dominance is body language that signals status and confidence, most notably open, expansive posture. People use it to look taller, larger and more attractive in person and in photos.
Research supports parts of this: status cues make people appear physically larger, and a PNAS study found expansive posture raised dating selection rates in speed-dates and an app experiment.

paras: In practice it means standing or sitting tall with open shoulders and taking up space, with relaxed movement. People apply it in photos, dates, interviews and gym settings.
There is little physical risk. In psychology the phrase also names a separate effect where nonverbal cues outweigh words, and over-assertive posture can be socially mismatched depending on context.

chain: Viewer perceives larger size and higher status
angle.text: Expansive posture changes how big and dominant someone looks, in person and in photos. Practitioners use it as a posture habit.

lead: Nonverbal dominance refers to body-language behaviour that signals status and power, such as expansive posture, open arms and taking up space. In looksmaxxing and dating circles it is treated as a free way to appear taller, bigger and more attractive.

Studies support some of these ideas. A 2009 PLOS ONE study found that nonverbal status cues increase perceived size, and postural openness was the cue most tied to this effect.[1] A 2016 PNAS study reported that postural expansiveness predicted romantic selection in speed-dating and in a GPS dating-app experiment with 3,000 participants, mediated by looking more dominant.[2]
In psychology the phrase "nonverbal dominance" also describes the tendency to trust nonverbal signals over words when they conflict, which varies between individuals.[3]
infobox: Psychology: nonverbal vs verbal cue weighting

paras: The PNAS studies found each unit of coded expansiveness nearly doubled the odds of a "yes" in speed-dating, and expansive photos were chosen more often in the app experiment.[2] The 2009 experiments found that high-status cues increase apparent size in the visible plane and that perceived size mediates perceived status.[1]
A 2014 randomized study found that people at higher risk for mania kept an expanded posture regardless of a partner posture, whereas low-risk people adapted complementarily.[4]
Cognitive research uses the term for how strongly a person weighs nonverbal cues over verbal ones; one study linked this to emotional intelligence.[3]
Experimental studies cited above are laboratory and field studies, not clinical trials of an intervention.[1][2][4]
